tracks.label: Opening
tracks.text: Chapter 3. Inside the Bird. Every spring, Bar-headed Geese (Anser indicus) that spend the winter on lakes and rivers in lowland India set off for breeding grounds in Central Asia, and the Himalayas stand in the way. When researchers fitted geese with GPS tags, they found that some birds crossed the range in a single day, typically climbing 4,000 to 6,000 meters in 7 to 8 hours. The highest reading came from one goose flying briefly at 7,290 meters. Mountaineers once reported geese passing high overhead, and the story grew that they fly over the summit of Everest; tracking has never shown that, because the birds mostly follow valleys and passes. Even so, at 5,500 meters each breath holds about half the oxygen it would at sea level, and the goose is flapping the whole way. The explanation lies inside the bird. Chapter 1 showed you the outside of a bird and its skeleton, and Chapter 2 showed how much energy flight demands. This chapter opens the body. You will see how air sacs drive air through the lungs in one direction, why birds run hot and how some of them deliberately cool down at night, how an animal with no teeth digests seeds and leaves, and how bird senses compare with ours, from color vision that reaches into the ultraviolet to the vultures and seabirds that find food by smell. Each system serves the same high-energy way of life. The ideas return in Chapter 5, where air moving through the syrinx makes song, and in Chapter 7, where fuel stores and the senses carry migrants across oceans.

tracks.label: 3.1 Breathing with air sacs
tracks.text: Section 3 point 1. Breathing with air sacs. As Chapter 2 showed, flapping flight is one of the most expensive things a vertebrate body can do, and every bit of that energy is released by burning fuel with oxygen. Your own lungs collect oxygen in a surprisingly wasteful way. Air travels down branching tubes into hundreds of millions of dead-end pockets, the alveoli, then comes back out the way it went in. Each new breath mixes with stale air left behind, so the air touching your blood is never fully fresh. Birds use a different design. Their lungs are small, stiff and fixed against the ribs, and they barely change volume. The pumping is done by a set of thin-walled air sacs, usually about nine of them, which fill much of the body cavity and in many species extend into the hollow bones you met in Chapter 1. The air sacs work like bellows. They have few blood vessels and take almost no part in gas exchange. Birds have no diaphragm. Instead, muscles swing the sternum and ribs down and forward to breathe in, enlarging the body cavity so the sacs expand, and draw them back to breathe out. The sacs fall into two groups: the caudal air sacs toward the rear of the body and the cranial air sacs toward the front. Between them lies the lung, threaded by many narrow, parallel tubes called parabronchi. From the wall of each parabronchus runs a dense network of tiny air capillaries, wound together with blood capillaries. This is where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it. Follow the air through a Rock Pigeon (Columba livia) in Figure 3.1. When the bird breathes in, most of the fresh air rushes down the trachea and the main bronchus, straight past the lung and into the caudal sacs; some enters the parabronchi directly. At the same moment, air that was already in the lung moves forward into the cranial sacs. When the bird breathes out, the caudal sacs squeeze their fresh air into the lung, and the cranial sacs empty their used air out through the trachea. The result is that air crosses the parabronchi in the same direction, from back to front, during both inhalation and exhalation. The lung is bathed in a nearly continuous stream of fresh air instead of a tide that comes and goes. Finding out which way air moves inside a living bird took new instruments. In 1971, William Bretz and Knut Schmidt-Nielsen at Duke University built small probes that register the direction of airflow and placed them at different points in the airways of ducks. During normal breathing, the readings showed the one-way pattern through the main gas-exchange tubes. Tracer-gas experiments that followed led to a popular summary: a single breath of air needs two full breathing cycles to pass through, into the caudal sacs on the first inhalation, through the lung on the first exhalation, into the cranial sacs on the second inhalation and out on the second exhalation. Treat this as an average route, not a strict queue, because inhaled air spreads and mixes along the way. Anatomists have searched for valves that could enforce the one-way flow and found none. The steering appears to come from the shape of the airway junctions and the momentum of the moving air, a mechanism called aerodynamic valving. The design has a second advantage. In the parabronchi, blood capillaries run across the air stream rather than alongside it, an arrangement called cross-current exchange. Blood leaving the lung has met the air at many points along the tube, so it can end up richer in oxygen than the air the bird breathes out, something a mammal lung cannot achieve. That edge matters most where oxygen is scarce. The Bar-headed Goose adds its own refinements to the general bird plan. Compared with lowland geese, it breathes more deeply in thin air, its hemoglobin binds oxygen more tightly, and its flight muscles are richer in capillaries, so oxygen moves more easily at each step from the air to the muscle cells. This breathing system is older than birds. In 2010, C. G. Farmer and Kent Sanders measured airflow in the lungs of American Alligators (Alligator mississippiensis), which have no air sacs, and found that air also moves one way through their lungs. The pattern persisted in lungs removed from the body, so it comes from the structure of the airways themselves. Crocodilians and birds are the two living branches of the archosaurs, so one-way airflow probably goes back to their common ancestor in the Triassic. Fossils supply the next piece. The vertebrae of the theropod dinosaur Majungasaurus, about 67 million years old, from Madagascar, carry openings in the same pattern that air sacs leave in the bones of living birds. This is evidence that bird-style air sacs were already present in non-avian theropods. A common misconception: Birds breathe in and out of their lungs just like we do, only faster. In fact, A bird’s lungs barely change volume. The air sacs do the pumping, and air flows one way through the parabronchi during both inhalation and exhalation. In mammals, air moves in and out of the same dead-end alveoli and mixes with stale air.

tracks.label: 3.2 Metabolism and body temperature
tracks.text: Section 3 point 2. Metabolism and body temperature. Birds are endotherms: like mammals, they make most of their body heat internally by burning food, and they hold a steady core temperature whatever the weather. They run hotter than we do. Most birds keep their core between about 38 and 42 degrees Celsius, usually a little higher during the active part of the day than at rest, compared with about 37 degrees Celsius in a human. A warm body has faster chemistry, so muscles contract quickly and nerves fire fast, which helps an animal that must react in flight. The cost is fuel. A bird’s metabolic rate, the rate at which it uses energy, is high even at rest and climbs steeply when it flies. Measuring that cost takes ingenuity. The standard method is to measure how much oxygen an animal uses, because each liter of oxygen consumed corresponds to a known amount of energy released. In 2019, Jessica Meir and colleagues raised Bar-headed Geese by hand from hatching, so that the birds imprinted on people, and trained them to fly in a wind tunnel while wearing masks that sampled their breath. In flight, the geese used energy about 16 times faster than at rest, and the extra oxygen was delivered mainly by more oxygen per heartbeat, with only a modest rise in heart rate. The team then lowered the oxygen in the air to match altitudes of 5,500 and 9,000 meters. In thin air the geese’s metabolic rate in flight fell below its level in normal air, and their heart rate did not climb any higher. Wild birds face the same budget. GPS tracking showed that Bar-headed Geese from lowland India can cross the Himalayas in a single day, typically climbing 4,000 to 6,000 meters in 7 to 8 hours, and that they tended to avoid the strong winds of the afternoon, climbing even in the still air of night. A later study implanted loggers that recorded heart rate, a stand-in for energy use, along with altitude. Flight cost rose quickly as the air thinned, so the geese followed the terrain, dropping into valleys and climbing again rather than holding a high altitude. In that study the geese spent most of their flight time below 6,000 meters, and the highest single record was a brief 7,290 meters. The circulation behind this effort resembles ours in one way: birds have a four-chambered heart that keeps oxygen-rich and oxygen-poor blood fully apart. Bird hearts are also, on average, larger for their body size than mammal hearts. Body size changes the budget. A small body has more surface for each gram of tissue, so it loses heat faster, and small birds must burn energy faster per gram to stay warm. Hummingbirds sit at the extreme: for their weight, hovering hummingbirds have some of the highest metabolic rates measured in any vertebrate. A Ruby-throated Hummingbird (Archilochus colubris) weighs about 3 grams, and by day it refuels with nectar and small insects many times an hour. A long, cool night without food is therefore a real danger, because the bird’s small fat store could run out before dawn. The solution is torpor, a controlled drop in body temperature and metabolic rate. On a cold night a hummingbird can let its body temperature fall far below its daytime level and cut its energy use sharply, then rewarm by shivering before it starts feeding again. The record holders are hummingbirds of the high Andes. In 2020, Blair Wolf and colleagues recorded a Black Metaltail (Metallura phoebe) whose body temperature fell to about 3.3 degrees Celsius during torpor, the lowest yet measured in a bird. One bird goes further still. In the 1940s the naturalist Edmund Jaeger found a Common Poorwill (Phalaenoptilus nuttallii) in a rock crevice in the California desert, cold and motionless, and it stayed torpid for weeks. The poorwill is still the only bird known to spend long stretches of the winter in a state close to hibernation. Holding a steady temperature also means getting rid of heat. Feathers are excellent insulation, and a cold bird fluffs them to trap more air and shivers to make heat. A hot bird does the reverse. Birds have no sweat glands, so they lose heat by evaporating water from the mouth and airways, either by panting or by rapidly vibrating the throat, a behavior called gular fluttering. Legs and feet pose their own problem, because they are thin and bare. In many birds, warm arteries running down the leg lie against cold veins coming back up, so heat passes from one to the other before it reaches the foot. This countercurrent heat exchange lets a gull stand on ice with cold feet while its core stays warm. A common misconception: A hummingbird found cold, fluffed up and unresponsive on a chilly morning must be dying. In fact, It is very likely in torpor, a normal energy-saving state. Its body temperature and metabolism have been turned down for the night, and it will rewarm by shivering and fly off. The best help is usually to leave it alone.

tracks.label: 3.3 Beaks, crops and gizzards
tracks.text: Section 3 point 3. Beaks, crops and gizzards. In Chapter 1 you saw that birds have no teeth: a keratin beak covers the jaws, and its shape is adapted to the diet. A beak can crack, tear, probe, filter or spear, but it cannot chew. Most birds swallow food whole or in pieces, and the processing that a mammal does in its mouth happens further down the digestive tract. An American Robin (Turdus migratorius) that tugs an earthworm from a lawn swallows it whole. In autumn and winter, when worms are harder to reach, robins eat far more fruit, and they swallow berries whole too. Figure 3.2 follows food from beak to cloaca. The first stop is the esophagus, a stretchy tube from mouth to stomach. In many birds, including pigeons, gamebirds, parrots, some finches, and hawks, eagles and falcons (but not owls), part of it is widened into a pouch called the crop. The crop is a storage bin. A pigeon on a busy sidewalk can fill its crop quickly and digest the meal later in safety, and you can sometimes see the bulge at the base of a well-fed pigeon’s neck. Not every bird has a crop, and in some it is only a slight widening. In our Rock Pigeon the crop has a second use. Both parents produce crop milk, a rich secretion made of fat- and protein-filled cells shed from the crop lining, and feed it to their young. Birds have a two-part stomach. The front part, the proventriculus, is glandular: it secretes acid and digestive enzymes that begin to break food down chemically. Food then passes to the gizzard, or ventriculus, a muscular grinding chamber with a tough, hard lining. In seed-eaters such as pigeons and sparrows the gizzard walls are thick and powerful, and the bird swallows small stones, called grit, which help crush hard seeds the way molars would. In birds that eat soft food such as fish, nectar or ripe fruit, the gizzard is thinner and less muscular. Owls show what the gizzard can sort. They swallow small mammals whole, digest the flesh and cough up compact pellets of fur and bone, which researchers pull apart to learn exactly what an owl has eaten. Diet can reshape the whole system. The Hoatzin (Opisthocomus hoazin) of South American river forests eats mostly leaves, a food few birds can use because plant cell walls are made of tough cellulose. In 1989, Alejandro Grajal and colleagues showed that the Hoatzin ferments leaves with bacteria in its enlarged crop and lower esophagus, the same strategy a cow uses in its rumen; it was the first bird known to digest food this way. Grit in the gizzard has a long history. Fossils of the small feathered dinosaur Caudipteryx, described in 1998, preserve clusters of stones in the stomach region, much like the grit of plant-eating birds today. The stones suggest that some of these dinosaurs, like many birds today, ground their food in a muscular gizzard. After the gizzard, food moves into the small intestine, where enzymes from the pancreas and bile from the liver finish digestion and nutrients are absorbed into the blood. Many birds have a pair of blind side pouches, the ceca, where the small and large intestines meet. They are largest in plant-eaters such as grouse, where bacteria inside them ferment tough plant fiber. The large intestine is short and ends in the cloaca, a single chamber that also receives the outputs of the kidneys and the reproductive tract. Birds excrete nitrogen waste mainly as uric acid, which needs little water to flush away; it is the white part of a bird dropping, and the dark part is feces. Fruit-eating birds pass seeds through quickly and drop them far from the parent plant, which makes them important seed dispersers. The gut can also change size. Organs are heavy, and a flying bird pays to carry every gram. Theunis Piersma and Robert Gill examined Bar-tailed Godwits (Limosa lapponica) that had died in Alaska, probably just after setting off on their nonstop flight across the Pacific to New Zealand, a journey you will study in Chapter 7. The birds carried huge fat stores, but their digestive organs, including the gizzard and intestines, were unusually small for birds of their size. Piersma and Gill concluded that the godwits had shrunk organs they would not use during the flight, trading digestive capacity for a lighter load. They titled their 1998 paper “Guts don’t fly”. A common misconception: Pigeons and chickens pecking at gravel are just picking it up by mistake. In fact, Many seed-eating birds swallow grit on purpose. The stones stay in the gizzard and help grind hard seeds, doing the job that teeth do in a mammal.

tracks.label: 3.4 Senses: vision, hearing and smell
tracks.text: Section 3 point 4. Senses: vision, hearing and smell. Birds are visual animals. Their eyes are very large for their heads; in many species the two eyes nearly meet in the middle of the skull, and an owl’s tube-shaped eyes can barely move in their sockets, which is why an owl turns its whole head to look around. The retina at the back of the eye is packed with light-sensing cells. Rods work in dim light. Cones work in bright light and detect color. Many birds have a fovea, a small pit where cones are packed most densely and vision is sharpest, and hawks, eagles and some other birds that judge distance at speed have two foveae in each eye. Human color vision rests on three types of cone, most sensitive to violet-blue, green and yellow-green light. Most birds have four types of single cone, so their color vision is tetrachromatic. The fourth type is sensitive to violet or ultraviolet light, wavelengths shorter than about 400 nanometers that we cannot see (Figure 3.3). In many songbirds and parrots this cone is most sensitive well into the ultraviolet; in others, such as chickens and most birds of prey, it peaks in the violet but still reaches into the ultraviolet. Most cones also hold a droplet of oil, usually colored, that filters light before it reaches the pigment, narrowing the range each cone responds to and sharpening color discrimination. Birds have double cones as well, thought to be used for judging brightness and motion rather than color. These facts come from a technique called microspectrophotometry. Researchers pass a tiny beam of light, one wavelength at a time, through a single cone cell from a bird’s retina and measure which wavelengths its pigment absorbs. Feathers tell the same story from the other side. Many plumages that look plain to us reflect strongly in the ultraviolet. The crown of the Blue Tit (Cyanistes caeruleus) of Europe looks blue to us, but instruments show that it also reflects ultraviolet light, and males and females, which look alike to a human observer, differ in that reflectance. Hearing matters too, above all for song, the subject of Chapter 5. Most birds hear best between about 1 and 4 kilohertz, roughly the range of their songs, and few hear much above 10 kilohertz, while a young human can hear up to about 20 kilohertz. Our running example uses its ears on the lawn. An American Robin hunting worms runs, stops and cocks its head. Because a robin’s eyes face sideways, the tilt was long read as looking. In experiments with captive robins, Robert Montgomerie and Patrick Weatherhead hid mealworms just under the soil surface and controlled which cues the birds could use. The robins still found prey when sound was the main cue available, evidence that they can hunt by ear as well as by eye. The Barn Owl (Tyto alba) is the champion listener. In experiments published in 1971, Roger Payne showed that Barn Owls could catch mice in a light-tight room, and that they would strike at a wad of paper dragged across the floor, which ruled out sight, body heat and smell as the cues. A Barn Owl’s ear openings sit at different heights on the two sides of its head, so a sound from below reaches one ear slightly differently than the other, and the dish-shaped disc of feathers around the face funnels sound toward the ears. Together these let the owl pinpoint prey both left to right and up and down in darkness. Smell was long thought to matter little to birds; in the 1800s John James Audubon concluded from experiments that vultures found carrion by sight. We now know that many birds smell well. The Turkey Vulture (Cathartes aura) has a large olfactory bulb and finds carcasses hidden under forest canopy by their odor. Pipeline workers have even located gas leaks by watching where Turkey Vultures gathered, because the gas carried an added odorant similar to the smell of decay. Kiwis, alone among birds, have nostrils at the tip of the bill and sniff out worms in the soil. At sea, many tubenoses, the group that includes albatrosses, petrels and shearwaters, can smell dimethyl sulfide, and some, such as storm-petrels and prions, are strongly drawn to it; the compound is released when krill and other small animals graze on plankton, so it leads the birds to rich feeding areas. A common misconception: Birds have almost no sense of smell. In fact, Many birds smell well. Turkey Vultures find hidden carcasses by odor, kiwis sniff for worms through nostrils at the tip of the bill, and many tubenoses track the smell of dimethyl sulfide across the ocean. The old view rested on a few early experiments and on studying mainly songbirds.
